Many examples of proton transfer reactions found in organic chemistry and bio- chemistry are described by the Brønsted–Lowry model. The various organic func- tional groups defined in Chapter 7 can participate in these reactions. Ethane (CH3CH3) is an extremely weak acid (see later) that can donate a proton to form its conjugate base CH3CH2

2, an example of a carbanion, a species that plays an important role in organic reaction mechanisms. Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) can donate a proton to form its conjugate base CH3CH2O2, another carbanion but one that is a much weaker base than the conjugate base of ethane. The carboxylic acids, of which acetic acid is an example, can give up the proton that is bonded to O (the so-called acidic proton) to form their anionic conjugated bases. Methylamine (CH3NH2) can accept a proton to form its conjugate acid the methylammonium ion (CH3NH1
3). The acid–base behavior of organic molecules is discussed in some detail in Section 15.8.
